title: Why Benaiah Chased a Lion Into a Pit on a Snowy Day
paragraphs: Why Benaiah Chased a Lion Into a Pit on a Snowy Day
Most people spend their lives running from lions.
Benaiah ran toward one.
Not in the sunshine. Not surrounded by soldiers. Not when conditions were safe.
On a snowy day. Inside a pit. Against a lion.
And somehow, buried inside one single verse, hidden in the shadows of King David’s mighty men, sits one of the most terrifying and revealing portraits of spiritual courage in all of Scripture.
The Bible says:

“And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was a valiant man of Kabzeel, a doer of great deeds. He struck down two heroes of Moab. He also went down and struck down a lion in a pit on a day when snow had fallen.” — 2 Samuel 23:20 (ESV)
At first glance, it almost sounds reckless.

Why would any sane man chase a lion into a pit? Why descend deeper into danger? Why fight where escape becomes nearly impossible? Why do it on a snowy day when footing is unstable and visibility is compromised?
Because some battles cannot be avoided.
And some destinies are only unlocked when a man stops running from what was sent to intimidate him.
The Hebrew language in this passage reveals something deeper than the English translation alone can fully capture.
The phrase “went down” comes from the Hebrew word יָרַד (yarad), meaning “to descend,” “to go downward,” or “to enter lower territory.” This was not an accidental encounter.
Benaiah intentionally descended.
The lion was below. Danger was below. Fear was below. Death was below.
And Benaiah chose to go there anyway.
That changes everything.
Most people pray for God to remove the pit. Very few ask God for courage to enter it.
But the entire Gospel story is built around descent.
Jesus descended into human suffering. He descended into rejection. He descended into grief. He descended into death itself.
Philippians 2:7 says Christ “emptied Himself.”
In Greek, the phrase is:
ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσεν (heauton ekenōsen)
From the word κενόω (kenoō), meaning “to empty,” “to pour out,” or “to lay aside status.”
Jesus did not stay where it was comfortable.
He came down.
And every real disciple eventually discovers the same terrifying truth:
There are places God will call you that feel beneath you.
Places where your pride dies. Places where your image dies. Places where your self-reliance dies. Places where excuses die. Places where hidden idols finally get exposed.
Some people are trying to rebuke the very pit God designed to transform them.
Benaiah understood something most believers still resist:
Victory often waits in the place your flesh least wants to enter.
The text also says it happened “on a snowy day.”
The Hebrew word for snow is שֶׁלֶג (sheleg).
Snow in the ancient Near East was uncommon in many regions and often represented harsh conditions, instability, danger, and vulnerability.
This was not ideal timing.
Benaiah did not postpone obedience until conditions improved.
That part hurts.
Because most people are waiting for a perfect season before they obey God.

“I’ll start praying seriously when life calms down.” “I’ll surrender fully when I heal first.” “I’ll forgive after they apologize.” “I’ll serve God after I fix myself.” “I’ll stop compromising eventually.”
But delayed obedience is still disobedience.
Benaiah did not negotiate with the weather.
He moved anyway.
Some of you have been waiting for emotional sunshine before confronting the lion that has stalked your life for years.

The lion of addiction. The lion of pornography. The lion of bitterness. The lion of secret sin. The lion of fear. The lion of depression. The lion of compromise. The lion of spiritual apathy. The lion of hidden hypocrisy.
And every day you delay, the lion grows more familiar with your patterns.
Scripture repeatedly uses lions as symbols of terror, destruction, and spiritual opposition.
1 Peter 5:8 says:
“Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour.”
The Greek phrase for “seeking someone to devour” is:
ζητῶν τίνα καταπίῃ (zētōn tina katapiē)
The word καταπίνω (katapinō) literally means “to swallow whole.”
Satan does not merely want influence. He wants consumption. He wants total destruction. He wants your identity. He wants your calling. He wants your purity. He wants your hunger for God.
And yet here is Benaiah…
Running toward the lion.
Not away.
There is a reason this story survived thousands of years.
Because every human being eventually stands at the edge of a pit.
The pit where fear says:
“If you go down there, you may not come back the same.”
And fear is right.
You won’t.

The version of you that loved comfort will not survive. The version of you addicted to approval will not survive. The version of you chained to secret compromise will not survive. The version of you pretending to trust God while secretly worshipping safety will not survive.
That is the point.
God never promised to preserve your flesh. He promised to transform your soul.
What makes this even more powerful is who Benaiah eventually became.
He was not merely some random warrior.
Benaiah later became commander over Solomon’s army.
The man who chased the lion eventually carried governmental authority.
The pit was preparation.
The lion was training.
The snowy day was the test.
And many people keep asking God for influence while avoiding the battles that create spiritual authority.
Nobody sees the hidden lions.
Nobody sees the midnight prayers. Nobody sees the tears. Nobody sees the private repentance. Nobody sees the warfare against temptation. Nobody sees the lonely obedience.
But heaven sees it.
David saw it.
And eventually, history remembered it.
One verse.
That is all Benaiah got.
One verse buried in a genealogy of warriors.
Yet thousands of years later, people still talk about the snowy pit.
Because courage leaves fingerprints eternity refuses to erase.
And maybe this is why this story grips the human heart so deeply.
Because everyone knows what it feels like to stare into something terrifying.
A diagnosis. A betrayal. A divorce. A funeral. A shattered dream. A hidden addiction. A season of unbearable loneliness. A prayer that feels unanswered.
There are moments where obedience feels like climbing into a pit with a lion.
Especially when God stays silent.
Especially when the snow keeps falling.
Especially when nobody else understands why you are still fighting.
But one of the greatest lies the enemy ever whispers is this:
“Your private battles do not matter.”
They matter more than you know.
The hidden victories shape public destinies.
This is why Jesus warned repeatedly about what happens in secret.
Matthew 6:6 says:
“But when you pray, go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret.”
The Greek word for “room” is ταμεῖον (tameion).
It referred to an inner chamber. A hidden place. A storage room.
God does His deepest work where applause cannot enter.
And perhaps your pit is not punishment.
Perhaps it is formation.
Perhaps the snowy day is not proof God abandoned you.
Perhaps it is proof heaven trusted you with a battle that would shape your future.
Benaiah teaches us something modern Christianity often forgets:
Faith is not passive.
Biblical faith moves.
Biblical faith confronts. Biblical faith obeys under pressure. Biblical faith advances while afraid. Biblical faith keeps descending even when the flesh begs to retreat.
And this matters because too many believers have built entire lives around avoiding discomfort.
Avoid conviction. Avoid sacrifice. Avoid surrender. Avoid accountability. Avoid repentance. Avoid spiritual discipline. Avoid the cross.
But Jesus never invited people into comfort.
He invited them into death.
Luke 9:23 says:
“If anyone would come after Me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow Me.”
The Greek word for “deny” is ἀπαρνέομαι (aparneomai).
It means to utterly disown. To refuse association. To reject ownership.
Jesus was not calling people to mild self-improvement.
He was calling them to crucifixion of the old self.
That is why so many people walked away from Him.
Real discipleship costs something.
And Benaiah’s story forces an uncomfortable question into the soul:
What lion are you still running from?
What conversation have you avoided? What sin have you protected? What compromise have you normalized? What fear has controlled your decisions? What act of obedience have you delayed?
Be honest. This hit harder than you expected.
Some of you have spent years praying for God to change your circumstances while refusing to confront the lion living inside your own heart.
But freedom often begins the moment you stop running.
The Gospel itself is proof.
At Calvary, Jesus stepped willingly into the pit humanity created.
Sin. Shame. Wrath. Death.
And unlike Benaiah, Jesus did not enter carrying His own guilt.
He entered carrying ours.
Isaiah 53:5 says:
“But He was pierced for our transgressions; He was crushed for our iniquities.”
The Hebrew word for “crushed” is דָּכָא (daka’).
It means shattered. Broken. Crushed down.
Jesus entered the deepest pit imaginable so sinners could be rescued from eternal separation from God.
The resurrection was heaven’s declaration that the Lion of Judah cannot be defeated.
Revelation 5:5 says:
“Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered.”
The Greek word used for conquered is νικάω (nikaō).
To overcome. To prevail. To triumph decisively.
This changes everything.
Because believers do not fight lions hoping Christ might win.
We fight from the position that Christ already conquered.
And maybe that is why Benaiah’s story still burns inside people.
Because deep down, everyone longs to become someone who stops retreating.

Someone who obeys even while trembling. Someone who stands firm when compromise is easier. Someone who trusts God when the snow keeps falling. Someone who keeps descending because they know God meets people in impossible places.
Some of you reading this are exhausted.
You have smiled publicly while bleeding privately. You have worshipped while grieving. You have prayed while doubting. You have fought battles nobody around you even noticed.
And maybe today God is reminding you:
The pit is not the end of your story.
The lion is not greater than the God who called you.
And the snow cannot stop what heaven already ordained.
Someone else reading your honesty may realize they are not alone.
One encounter with the lion may become the moment heaven introduces you to who you were always called to be.
